title: The definite integral as an area under a curve
topicTitle: The definite integral as an area under a curve
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Area Becomes a Limit

**The definite integral as area under a curve**: Riemann sums, the limit definition, and the Fundamental Theorem that makes evaluation algebraic.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The area problem

- Area under y = f(x) ≥ 0 from a to b: partition [a, b] into n subintervals, erect rectangles of height f(xᵢ*), sum the areas — the **Riemann sum** Σf(xᵢ*)Δxᵢ. Refine: **∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = lim_{n→∞} Σ f(xᵢ*)Δx** — the definite integral.
- **Notation:** ∫ (elongated S for sum), a and b the limits, dx the width differential.

### 2.2 Signed area

- The integral counts area **above the axis positively, below negatively**: ∫ can be zero (cancelling lobes) or negative — "area under the curve" means *signed* area; true geometric area needs |f|.

### 2.3 Properties of the definite integral

- **Linearity:** ∫(af + bg) = a∫f + b∫g. **Additivity:** ∫ₐᵇ + ∫ᵦᶜ = ∫ₐᶜ. **Reversal:** ∫ᵇₐ = −∫ₐᵇ. **Same limits:** 0. **Domination:** f ≤ g ⟹ ∫f ≤ ∫g. **Estimate:** m(b−a) ≤ ∫ ≤ M(b−a).

### 2.4 The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

- **Part 1:** if f is continuous, F(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t)dt satisfies **F′(x) = f(x)** — differentiation undoes integration.
- **Part 2 (evaluation theorem):** ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = **F(b) − F(a)** for any anti-derivative F — the bridge from limit to algebra. Constants cancel: any anti-derivative works.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Riemann sum** | Rectangle-area total | Σf(xᵢ*)Δx |
| **Definite integral** | Limit of Riemann sums | ∫ₐᵇ f dx |
| **Signed area** | Above +, below − | sine over a period = 0 |
| **FTC Part 2** | F(b) − F(a) | evaluation bridge |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why the limit definition matters

- The Riemann limit is the *definition* — it makes "area under a curve" precise for curved boundaries where geometry fails, and it is the license for every property (linearity, additivity) proved from sums.

### 4.2 FTC as the dictionary

- Part 1: the accumulation function ∫ₐˣ f(t)dt is an anti-derivative of f — integration builds derivatives. Part 2: evaluation needs only one anti-derivative — the constant C cancels, which is why definite integrals need no +C.

### 4.3 The definite-integral workflow

- Find any anti-derivative F (indefinite-integral skills), compute F(b) − F(a), done. The upper-minus-lower order matters: reversing limits flips the sign.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Indefinite vs definite**

| Feature | Indefinite ∫f dx | Definite ∫ₐᵇ f dx |
|---|---|---|
| Output | family F + C | number |
| Meaning | anti-derivative | signed area |
| Constant | required | cancels |
| Tool | table/rules | FTC Part 2 |

## 6. Common Confusions

**No +C in definite integrals:** the evaluation theorem subtracts — constants cancel by construction.
**Negative integrals are fine:** f < 0 gives ∫ < 0 — signed area; geometric area needs ∫|f|.
**Limits order:** ∫ᵇₐ = −∫ₐᵇ — flipping the limits flips the sign.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB 2022 (verified PYQ): Evaluate ∫₀¹ x² dx. (2m)** — **Anti-derivative:** F(x) = x³/3. **FTC Part 2:** ∫₀¹ x²dx = F(1) − F(0) = 1/3 − 0 = **1/3**. (Geometric check: the area under the parabola from 0 to 1 is a third of the unit square — Archimedes knew this by exhaustion.)

**NEB-style (3m): Compute ∫₀^π sin x dx and interpret.** — **Anti-derivative:** −cos x. **Evaluate:** [−cos x]₀^π = (−cos π) − (−cos 0) = 1 + 1 = **2**. **Interpretation:** the sine hump above the axis from 0 to π has signed area 2 — the full period ∫₀^{2π} = 0 because the two humps cancel (signed area).

**NEB-style (3m): Show from the definition that ∫ₐᵇ c dx = c(b − a).** — Partition [a, b]: every rectangle has height c and width Δxᵢ; the Riemann sum = Σc·Δxᵢ = c·ΣΔxᵢ = c(b − a) exactly — for **every** n, so the limit is c(b − a) ∎. Constant functions are the case where the sum never changes: no refinement needed.

The power rule for integration fails at n = -1, so int 1/x dx = ln|x| + C keeps the absolute value bars, and the integrand is undefined at x = 0.

int_a^b f(x)dx depends on the limits as well as on f, so two different integrals of the same function can differ in value and even in sign.

practiceQuestions: **NEB 2022 (verified PYQ): Evaluate ∫₀¹ x² dx. (2m)** — **Anti-derivative:** F(x) = x³/3 (power rule reversed). **FTC Part 2 (evaluation theorem):** ∫₀¹ x²dx = [x³/3]₀¹ = F(1) − F(0) = **1/3 − 0 = 1/3**. **No +C:** any constant in F cancels in the subtraction — definite integrals are numbers, not families. **Geometric reading:** the region under y = x² from 0 to 1 fills exactly one-third of the unit square — the fact Archimedes established by exhaustion two millennia before limits had a name.

**NEB-style (3m): Compute ∫₀^π sin x dx and interpret the result as signed area.** — **Anti-derivative:** ∫sin x dx = −cos x. **Evaluate:** ∫₀^π sin x dx = [−cos x]₀^π = (−cos π) − (−cos 0) = (−(−1)) − (−1) = 1 + 1 = **2**. **Interpretation:** the single sine hump between 0 and π lies entirely **above** the axis, so its signed area is positive — exactly 2 square units. **Contrast:** over a full period, ∫₀^{2π} sin x dx = [−cos x]₀^{2π} = (−1) − (−1) = **0** — the upper hump (+2) and the lower trough (−2) cancel: the definite integral measures **signed** area, and symmetric oscillation integrates to nothing.

**NEB-style (3m): Using the definition of the definite integral as a limit of Riemann sums, show that ∫ₐᵇ c dx = c(b − a) for any constant c.** — **Setup:** partition [a, b] into n subintervals with widths Δxᵢ and any sample points xᵢ*. **Riemann sum:** since f(x) = c for every x, every rectangle has height c: Σ f(xᵢ*)Δxᵢ = Σ c·Δxᵢ = **c·ΣΔxᵢ = c(b − a)** — the widths telescope to the full interval length. **Limit:** the sum equals c(b − a) for *every* partition and every n — the sequence is constant, so its limit is c(b − a) ∎. **Reading:** constant functions are the degenerate case where refinement changes nothing; the formula ∫ₐᵇ c dx = c(b − a) is also the m(b − a) ≤ ∫ ≤ M(b − a) estimate with m = M = c, binding tight.

mcs.question: The value of the definite integral from 0 to pi of sin x dx is
mcs.explanation: An antiderivative of sin x is -cos x, so the value is -cos(pi) - (-cos 0) = 1 - (-1) = 2. The value 0 is the trap of writing the answer as cos(b) - cos(a).

mcs.question: The value of the definite integral from 1 to e of (1/x) dx is
mcs.explanation: An antiderivative of 1/x is ln|x|, so the value is ln(e) - ln(1) = 1 - 0 = 1.

mcs.question: The area of the region bounded by the curves y = x and y = x^2 is
mcs.explanation: The curves meet where x = x^2, that is at x = 0 and x = 1, and x lies above x^2 in between, so the area is the integral of (x - x^2) from 0 to 1, which is 1/2 - 1/3 = 1/6.

mcs.question: For every integrable function f, the definite integral from a to a of f(x) dx equals
mcs.explanation: An interval of zero length encloses no area, so the integral is 0. This also follows from F(a) - F(a) = 0 by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

mcs.question: If f(x) is negative on part of the interval [a, b], the total geometric area between the curve and the x-axis is given by
options: the integral from a to b of f(x) dx
the integral from a to b of |f(x)| dx
the integral from b to a of f(x) dx
minus the integral from a to b of f(x) dx
mcs.explanation: The definite integral counts the region below the axis negatively, so it gives a net area. Taking the absolute value of the integrand turns every contribution positive and yields the total geometric area.

numericals:
**1. [Idea: an integral with a shifted inner function where the bounds must transform]** Evaluate $\int_0^1 \dfrac{2x}{(x^2+1)^3}\,dx$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Let $u = x^2+1$, so $du = 2x\,dx$. The limits transform: $x=0 \Rightarrow u=1$, and $x=1 \Rightarrow u=2$.
ewline
ewlineThe integral becomes$
ewline\int_1^2 u^{-3}du = \left[ rac{u^{-2}}{-2}ight]_1^2 = - rac12\left[ rac{1}{u^2}ight]_1^2 = - rac12\left( rac14 - 1ight) =  rac{3}{8}$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $ rac38$.
ewline
ewline**Trap:** keeping limits $0$ and $1$ while integrating with respect to $u$. That gives $\left[- rac{1}{2u^2}ight]_0^1$, which is undefined at $u=0$ — the tell-tale sign that the substitution was mishandled.

**2. [Idea: by parts where the LIATE rule chooses the log term as $u$]** Evaluate $\int x\ln x\,dx$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** By parts, $\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du$.$^{ ullet}$ **LIATE** orders: Logarithmic before Algebraic, so take $u=\ln x$ and $dv=x\,dx$. Then $du= rac{dx}{x}$ and $v= rac{x^2}{2}$.
ewline
ewline$
ewline\int x\ln x\,dx =  rac{x^2}{2}\ln x - \int  rac{x^2}{2}\cdot rac{dx}{x} =  rac{x^2}{2}\ln x -  rac12\int x\,dx =  rac{x^2}{2}\ln x -  rac{x^2}{4} + C$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $ rac{x^2}{2}\ln x -  rac{x^2}{4}+C$, for $x>0$.
ewline
ewline**What went wrong if $u$ is chosen wrongly:** taking $u=x$, $dv=\ln x\,dx$ needs $\int \ln x\,dx$ first, which is itself an integral by parts — the problem gets strictly harder. **Also note:** on $[0,1]$ this integral is a proper one and $\int_0^1 x\ln x\,dx$ converges even though $\ln 0$ is undefined, since $x\ln x 	o 0$.

**3. [Idea: repeated by parts that must be stopped at a vanishing term]** Evaluate $\int x^2 e^x\,dx$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:**$^{ ullet}$ 1st application, $u=x^2$, $dv=e^x dx$, $du=2x\,dx$, $v=e^x$:$
ewline I = x^2e^x - 2\int xe^x\,dx$.$^{ ullet}$ 2nd application to the remaining integral, $u=x$, $dv=e^x dx$:$
ewline\int xe^x dx = xe^x - e^x$.
ewline
ewlineSubstitute back:$^{
ewline}I = x^2e^x - 2(xe^x - e^x) = x^2e^x - 2xe^x + 2e^x = e^x(x^2 - 2x + 2) + C$.
ewline
ewline**Verify by differentiating:** $ rac{d}{dx}\left[e^x(x^2-2x+2)ight] = e^x(x^2-2x+2) + e^x(2x-2) = e^x\cdot x^2$. ✓
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $e^x(x^2-2x+2)+C$. **The stopping rule:** stop as soon as a term becomes $0$; had a fourth application been attempted it would be meaningless.

**4. [Idea: symmetry collapses the work before any integration happens]** Evaluate $\int_{-2}^{2}\left(x^3\cos x + \sqrt{4-x^2}ight)dx$.
ewline
ewline**Solution: split by parity first.**$^{ ullet}$ $x^3$ is ODD and $\cos x$ is EVEN, so $x^3\cos x$ is ODD. An odd function integrates to $0$ over $[-2,2]$:$
ewline\int_{-2}^2 x^3\cos x\,dx = 0$.$^{ ullet}$ $\sqrt{4-x^2}$ is EVEN, so by King's rule $\int_{-2}^{2}\sqrt{4-x^2}\,dx = 2\int_0^2 \sqrt{4-x^2}\,dx$.
ewline
ewlineThis remaining integral is the area of a quarter circle of radius 2:$
ewline\int_0^2\sqrt{4-x^2}\,dx =  rac14 \pi(2)^2 = \pi$.
ewline
ewlineSo the total is $0 + 2\pi$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $2\pi$. **The idea:** the odd part was dispatched with no calculus at all. Attempting to integrate $x^3\cos x$ directly needs repeated by parts for nothing.

**5. [Idea: the bounds do not determine the top curve — solve the intersection first]** Find the area bounded by $y=x^2$ and $y=\sqrt{x}$ for $x \ge 0$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Find the intersections: $x^2 = \sqrt{x} \Rightarrow x^4 = x \Rightarrow x(x^3-1)=0$, so $x=0$ and $x=1$.
ewline
ewline**Determine which is on top.** At $x= rac12$: $y_1 = x^2 =  rac14$ and $y_2 = \sqrt{x} =  rac{1}{\sqrt2} \approx 0.707$. Since $\sqrt{x} > x^2$ there, $\sqrt{x}$ is the TOP curve.
ewline
ewline**Area:**$^{ ullet}$ $\displaystyle A = \int_0^1 \left(\sqrt{x} - x^2ight)dx = \left[ rac{2}{3}x^{3/2} -  rac{x^3}{3}ight]_0^1 =  rac23 -  rac13 =  rac13$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $ rac13$ square units. **Trap:** integrating $x^2-\sqrt{x}$ and getting $- rac13$. The top-minus-bottom convention means a negative answer signals the curves were named backwards, not that the area is negative.

**6. [Idea: the region is split because the bounding curve changes]** Find the area enclosed by $y=2x+1$, $y=x^2+2$ and the $y$-axis.
ewline
ewline**Solution:**$^{ ullet}$ The two curves meet where $2x+1 = x^2+2$, i.e. $x^2-2x+1=0$, i.e. $(x-1)^2=0$, so they are **tangent at $x=1$**, meeting at $(1,3)$.
ewline
ewline$^{ ullet}$ At $x=0$ the line gives $1$ and the parabola $2$, so the LINE is on top for $0\le x \le 1$ (tangent means they only just touch at $x=1$).$^{ ullet}$ The $y$-axis closes the region at $x=0$.
ewline
ewline**Area:**$^{ ullet}$ $\displaystyle A = \int_0^1 \left[(2x+1)-(x^2+2)ight]dx = \int_0^1\left(-x^2+2x-1ight)dx = \left[- rac{x^3}{3}+x^2-xight]_0^1 = - rac13+1-1 = - rac13$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** area $=  rac13$ square units (the negative integral confirms the curves were named the wrong way round, so the true area is $ rac13$). **Note:** tangency gives a single intersection, so only one integral is needed — but the sign check is what catches the reversal.

**NEB-style (3m): Using the definition of the definite integral as a limit of Riemann sums, show that ∫ₐᵇ c dx = c(b − a) for any constant c.** — **Setup:** partition [a, b] into n subintervals with widths Δxᵢ and any sample points xᵢ*. **Riemann sum:** since f(x) = c for every x, every rectangle has height c: Σ f(xᵢ*)Δxᵢ = Σ c·Δxᵢ = **c·ΣΔxᵢ = c(b − a)** — the widths telescope to the full interval length. **Limit:** the sum equals c(b − a) for *every* partition and every n — the sequence is constant, so its limit is c(b − a) ∎. **Reading:** constant functions are the degenerate case where refinement changes nothing; the formula ∫ₐᵇ c dx = c(b − a) is also the m(b − a) ≤ ∫ ≤ M(b − a) estimate with m = M = c, binding tight.

examples: ***The cancelling lobes*** - sine over a full period integrates to 0: the hump above the axis and the trough below cancel - signed area in action.
universalFacts: Odometer trip distance is a definite integral of speed from start to finish time - F(b) - F(a) with the starting point as the lower limit.
